title: DirectMeds compounded semaglutide/tirzepatide 'same active ingredient' claims
ad_content:
If you’ve looked into brand-name versions of semaglutide, you know the cost can be steep – especially without insurance. That’s where buying compounded semaglutide online can make a big difference. Compounded medications are created by licensed compounding pharmacies using the same active ingredients.
Compounded semaglutide contains the same active ingredient as branded semaglutide.
Don’t give up hope if brand-name Mounjaro is out of reach due to cost. You may be able to get compounded tirzepatide online, which is an effective and budget-friendly alternative. Compounded formulations use the same active ingredient as the brand-name drug, customized by licensed compounding pharmacies to meet your needs.

expected_findings.claim: If you’ve looked into brand-name versions of semaglutide, you know the cost can be steep – especially without insurance. That’s where buying compounded semaglutide online can make a big difference. Compounded medications are created by licensed compounding pharmacies using the same active ingredients.
Compounded semaglutide contains the same active ingredient as branded semaglutide.

Don’t give up hope if brand-name Mounjaro is out of reach due to cost. You may be able to get compounded tirzepatide online, which is an effective and budget-friendly alternative. Compounded formulations use the same active ingredient as the brand-name drug, customized by licensed compounding pharmacies to meet your needs.

notes: FDA CDER Warning Letter MARCS-CMS 716822, dated September 9, 2025, signed George Tidmarsh (CDER Director); FDA reviewed https://directmeds.com in August 2025. ad_content = the three bulleted claims under 'The following claims concerning compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide products appear on your website:', verbatim, one per line. Letter reasoning: 'Compounded drug products are not FDA-approved. Your claims imply that your products are the same as an FDA-approved product when they are not.' Letter cites only FDCA 502(a)/502(bb), 301(a), 301(c) (no 21 CFR 202.1). Footnote 2: 'Overstatements of efficacy or minimization of risk are of particular concern and may constitute misbranding.' 'an effective and budget-friendly alternative' also arguably overstates efficacy (footnote 2), but the letter's stated basis is sameness to an FDA-approved product.

title: Elevated compounded GLP-1 'personalized versions' and Semaglutide ODT claims
company: Elevate Your Wellness LLC, dba Elevated
ad_content:
Compounded GLP-1 medications are personalized versions of treatments like Semaglutide or Tirzepatide. They’re made by licensed compounding pharmacies based on a prescription from a qualified healthcare provider. They contain the same active ingredient as the branded medications, but are compounded to offer a more personalized and often more accessible option.
Semaglutide ODT is a custom-formulated, dissolvable tablet that delivers the same active ingredient found in the leading GLP-1 weight loss medications – without the need for injections.

notes: FDA CDER Warning Letter MARCS-CMS 715801, dated September 9, 2025; FDA reviewed https://www.getfitmedical.com in August 2025. ad_content = the four bulleted product headings the letter says 'appear on webpages that offer only compounded products', verbatim. Spans mens_health (sildenafil/tadalafil) and weight_loss (semaglutide/tirzepatide); vertical set to mens_health. Letter reasoning: 'Compounded drug products are not FDA-approved. Your claims imply that your products are the same as an FDA-approved product when they are not.' Letter cites only FDCA 502(a)/502(bb), 301(a), 301(c) (no 21 CFR 202.1). Footnote 2: 'Overstatements of efficacy or minimization of risk are of particular concern and may constitute misbranding.' Calling a compounded drug 'GENERIC' implies an FDA-approved generic (ANDA), so false_fda_approval_claim is a defensible secondary label.

title: FDA consumer page on compounded GLP-1s (accurate disclosure language control)
ad_content:
FDA is aware that some patients and health care professionals may look to unapproved versions of GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists) drugs, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, as an option for weight loss. This can be risky for patients, as unapproved versions do not undergo FDA’s review for safety, effectiveness and quality before they are marketed.
[…]
Compounded drugs should only be used in patients whose medical needs cannot be met by an FDA-approved drug.
Patients should obtain a prescription from their doctor and fill the prescription at a state-licensed pharmacy.
Visit FDA’s BeSafeRx campaign for resources to safely buy prescription medicines online.
Talk to your doctor if you have questions about your medicines.
[…]
Look for these warning signs, including if a company:
makes claims such as the compounded drug is the same as an FDA-approved drug
offers medicine at deep discounts or prices that seem too good to be true
sends medicine that looks different than what you’ve previously received at your local pharmacy or was pictured on their website, or arrives in packaging that is broken or damaged or lacks instructions for use
does not require a screening and prescription by a licensed doctor before providing medicine
does not have a licensed doctor available to answer questions after you receive your medication
[…]
A compounded drug might be appropriate if a patient’s medical need cannot be met by an FDA-approved drug, or the FDA-approved drug is not commercially available. However, compounded drugs are not FDA approved. This means the agency does not review compounded drugs for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed.
[…]
Some of the adverse events are serious and some patients reported seeking medical attention for their symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and constipation.
must_not_flag: compounded drugs are not FDA approved
This means the agency does not review compounded drugs for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed.
unapproved versions do not undergo FDA’s review for safety, effectiveness and quality before they are marketed

Compounded drugs should only be used in patients whose medical needs cannot be met by an FDA-approved drug.
makes claims such as the compounded drug is the same as an FDA-approved drug

notes: Real published text, verbatim excerpts (non-contiguous blocks joined with '[…]') from FDA's page 'FDA’s Concerns with Unapproved GLP-1 Drugs Used for Weight Loss' (Drug Alerts and Statements; 'Content current as of: 10/01/2026'; opened 2026-11-17). Blocks come from 'Understanding unapproved versions of these drugs', 'FDA recommendations for health care professionals and patients', 'Telehealth red flags for consumers', 'Concerns with compounded versions of these drugs', and 'Dosing concerns with compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide'. Chosen per scope change (no synthetic data): it is the disclosure language fda-001..005 lacked, and it is US-government public-domain text, so it can be stored verbatim. It is consumer guidance, not an ad. Hard negative: it quotes the prohibited 'same as an FDA-approved drug' idea and the 'prescription by a licensed doctor' gate only as warnings; a reviewer that keyword-matches would wrongly flag it. Not used: wegovy.com branded copy with ISI was opened and fits, but it is Novo Nordisk copyrighted text and was not reproduced at length.
